own_scenes.desc: Los hermanos Bryan «Birdman» y Ronald «Slim» Williams, del Magnolia y de la escena bounce, fundaron Cash Money en 1991 con U.N.L.V., Kilo-G y las bases de Mannie Fresh, que tocaba con músicos en directo sobre la caja de ritmos. Ficharon a Juvenile y a los adolescentes Lil Wayne, B.G. y Turk y sacaron treinta y un discos en seis años vendidos en tiendas como Peaches. Wendy Day (Rap Coalition) les hizo un plan de negocio y los vendió como «el próximo No Limit»: en 1998 Universal firmó un 80-20 con los másteres de vuelta a los tres años. 400 Degreez de Juvenile («Ha», con remix de Jay-Z, y «Back That Azz Up») y «Bling Bling» de B.G. con los Hot Boys (la palabra llegó al Oxford English Dictionary): eran los ostentosos, frente a los soldados de No Limit. Hubo quejas por el dinero, pero Lil Wayne se volvió un gran letrista con sus mixtapes y su Young Money fichó a Drake y Nicki Minaj.

refs.q: I respect you because you’re the only motherfucker from New York that came to my backyard.
refs.para: There was a number on the back of the CD that said, For bookings, call this number. So I called the number, and that’s how I initiated the first meeting with Baby and Slim. I remember the first thing that Baby said to me when he met me was, “I respect you because you’re the only motherfucker from New York that came to my backyard.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 18: The South Got Something to Say

refs.q: For them, it was the stuntas—the people hustling that are showing rings and cars and jewelry.
refs.para: That was the difference of us and Cash Money. Even though they artists were so hard—Juvenile, they were hard artists, gangsters—“Bling” gave them a new look. For [No Limit], we were the underdogs, the soldiers, the riders. For them, it was the stuntas—the people hustling that are showing rings and cars and jewelry. They gave life to that, but we were different.
